analysis.title: THINK Ahead: This is how bad European inflation could get this winter
key_insights: ING's James Smith argues the sharp rise in European natural gas prices is a serious inflation headache even though markets and the ECB are focused on France and bond yields. Oil and gas prices have both exceeded the ECB's 'adverse' scenario from its September projections.
Oil prices and two-year swap rates have decoupled since mid-September, when the French political and fiscal turmoil started. Oil is no longer driving rate pricing.

The episode is becoming a natural gas crisis as well as an oil crisis, and looks more like 2022 than it did earlier in the summer. In percentage terms the gas price rise is larger than at the equivalent point in the Ukraine shock, although the absolute level is far below the 2022 peak.

ING sees 4% eurozone inflation this winter as increasingly baked in. Eurozone inflation hit 3.8% in September and UK inflation 3.5%. Inflation is unlikely to return to 2% by spring or early summer, though the 2026 oil spike dropping out of the annual comparison from April offsets some of the gas effect.

UK household energy bills (price cap) are expected to rise about 25% in January. By next summer the energy category should add roughly one percentage point more to UK inflation than it does today. Eurozone household energy prices follow a similar pattern, and bills are unlikely to peak until after winter.
Eurozone inflation reaches 5% in ING's scenario analysis if oil is at $130/bbl and gas stays at current levels.

Eurozone consumer food inflation is only 1.1%, versus a peak near 20% in the last episode. Fresh food picked up in September, driven by 'fruit-bearing vegetables', while import and producer output food prices remain in deflation. ING expects this to change and calls it the main item to watch in October inflation data due late next week. The ECB sees food inflation peaking near 3.5% next summer, with drought, a coming El Nino and rising agricultural prices as uncertainties.

Second-round effects across the broader basket are what would matter for the ECB, and there is still no evidence of them. Energy-intensive inflation categories show no pressure, but they tend to lag energy inflation by about six months, so effects should start to appear now. Other upside risks are AI investment bottlenecks, a resurgence in the jobs market and widespread government energy support packages. None of these is ING's base case.

If the ECB hikes in December it would be acting as insurance against a repeat of 2022, not on evidence of broad inflation pressure from the Iran war. ING expects headline inflation to have peaked by spring and does not expect second-round effects at scale. ING is not forecasting further ECB hikes next year and sees a possible rate cut by next Christmas.

US: the Fed is expected to hold on Wednesday. Jefferson, Bowman and Waller signal another hike is likely but not urgent, and Chair Warsh did not talk up action at the IMF meetings in Bangkok, unlike at Jackson Hole before the September hike. ING still expects a December hike given strong growth, low unemployment and above-target inflation.
US 3Q GDP (Thursday) is expected at 3.4% annualised, driven by consumer spending and tech investment. Core PCE is expected at +0.3% m/m, which supports ING's December hike call.

Canada: the Bank of Canada decision (Wednesday) is a close call, and ING leans to a hold because inflation was softer than expected, jobs were lost, unemployment is elevated and the environment is 'risk off'. ING says a hike is still coming.

Eurozone: the ECB is very likely to stay on hold at its October meeting because of the French fiscal and political crisis and higher bond yields, and will delay the next hike decision to December. The September message was surprisingly hawkish. Eurozone 3Q GDP is estimated near 0.3% q/q after 0.6% in 2Q, with October sentiment likely weaker on renewed energy price rises.

France: 3Q GDP is expected to stagnate after zero growth in 2Q and a 0.2% contraction in 1Q. Industrial output fell in July and August, goods consumption fell 0.5% in August, and rising borrowing costs, protests and violence weigh on confidence.

Food inflation could rise sharply, with drought, a coming El Nino and rising agricultural commodity prices as drivers.

French fiscal and political stress and higher bond yields constrain the ECB and weigh on investment and confidence.

tension_points.bull_case: Headline inflation should peak by spring as the oil spike drops out of the annual comparison. ING does not expect second-round effects at scale, so it forecasts no more ECB hikes next year and a possible cut by next Christmas.
tension_points.bear_case: Energy-intensive categories lag energy inflation by about six months, so second-round effects may only now begin. Gas prices are up more in percentage terms than at the same point in the Ukraine shock, and food, AI bottlenecks, jobs and energy support are upside risks.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Evidence of second-round effects materialising at scale across the broader inflation basket by spring, or oil at $130/bbl with gas unchanged taking inflation to 5%.
